column2: The nearest people were at the whaling stations on South Georgia. 1,300 kilometres away, across the Southern Ocean.
Shackleton decided to go for help in the biggest lifeboat, the James Caird, about seven metres long.
He took five men with him. Frank Worsley to navigate, Tom Crean, the carpenter Harry McNish, and two sailors, Timothy McCarthy and John Vincent.
On the twenty-fourth of April 1916, they pushed off. Twenty-two men watched them go.
They sailed through one of the roughest seas on Earth, in waves as tall as buildings.
They took turns, four hours at the helm, four hours trying to sleep in a soaking space under the canvas.
Worsley found their way with a sextant, catching the sun when it showed for a few seconds through the clouds.
Ice formed on the boat and made it top-heavy. They had to crawl out and chip it off before it rolled them over.
After sixteen days, they saw South Georgia. Then a hurricane hit, and nearly threw them onto the rocks.
On the tenth of May 1916, they landed in King Haakon Bay. They had made it.
